data.text/html:
Google Maps is unreasonably fast: shortest paths, from Dijkstra to contraction hierarchies

An interactive companion to Veritasium's "Google Maps is unreasonably fast. Let me explain".
New York to San Francisco: more than 64 million intersections and roughly ||(10^{220}||) possible routes. Your phone finds the best one in about four seconds. How?

data.text/markdown: How to read the pictures. Every widget in this notebook uses the same colors: green ring = source, red ring = target, orange = frontier (we know a cost, but it might still drop), blue = explored from the source (cost is final), purple = explored from the target (backward search), gold = the shortest path, and dashed brown = shortcut (an edge that isn't a real road). The video's order is the notebook's order: brute force → BFS → Dijkstra → A* → travel time → bidirectional → hierarchies → contraction hierarchies.

0 · Why you can't just try every route

The simplest "algorithm" is to list every route and keep the shortest. Picture a city of ||(n\times n||) blocks and only allow routes that always head east or north (never backtrack). Each route is a sequence of ||(n||) "east" moves and ||(n||) "north" moves, so there are ||[\#\text{routes} = \binom{2n}{n} \approx \frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi n}}.||]That number explodes. The video's estimate for the real North American network, with backtracking-free routes from New York to San Francisco, is about ||(10^{220}||). At a billion routes per second, that's more than ||(10^{200}||) years.

At what n do you cross the red line? A whole continent's intersections only fit in a tiny city of a few\nhundred blocks per side. \u003cstrong\u003eEnumerating routes is hopeless. We need an algorithm that never looks at most of them.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
1 · Rotterdam → Groningen: breadth-first search, then Dijkstra's 20-minute idea

In 1956 Dijkstra needed a demo for the ARMAC computer that non-mathematicians could understand: what's the shortest way to travel from Rotterdam to Groningen? Below is a simplified graph of the Netherlands. The nodes are cities, the edges are roads, and the numbers are distances in units of about 10 km. Breadth-first search (BFS) explores every node 1 step away, then 2 steps away, and so on. It finds the path with the fewest edges, because it treats every road as the same length. Dijkstra's algorithm keeps a cost for every node: the shortest distance found so far from the source. It starts with ||(\text{cost}(s)=0||) and ||(\infty||) everywhere else. Then it repeats:
  1. pick the unexplored node ||(u||) with the lowest cost and mark it explored;
  2. for every neighbour ||(v||), relax the edge: ||(\;\text{cost}(v) \leftarrow \min\big(\text{cost}(v),\ \text{cost}(u) + w(u,v)\big)||).
You can stop when the target is the cheapest unexplored node. By then every path cheaper than it has been explored.

data.text/markdown:
2 · A*: punish the illogical directions

On a big map, Dijkstra is fast but wasteful. Going from Newark Airport to the Central Park Zoo, it explores all 10 km journeys, then all 20 km journeys, and so on, which includes Staten Island and large parts of New Jersey: about 65,000 nodes. It spreads out in every direction, even directly away from the target. A* is Dijkstra with one change. Nodes are ordered by their cost plus a guess of the remaining distance: ||[f(v) = \underbrace{\text{cost}(v)}_{\text{known, from source}} + \; w\cdot\underbrace{h(v)}_{\text{straight-line distance to target}}||]Polylog's picture from the video: lift every node to a height equal to its straight-line distance from the target. Moving uphill (away from the target) now costs extra, so the search rolls downhill toward the target. With ||(w = 0||) you get plain Dijkstra. With ||(w = 1||) the guess never overestimates the true distance, so A* still returns the shortest path. With ||(w > 1||) the slope is steeper and the search is more aggressive, but it may return a path that is not the shortest. On a grid where you can only step up, down, left, or right, the straight-line guess is the Manhattan distance ||(|\Delta r| + |\Delta c|||).

data.text/markdown:
3 · Shortest doesn't mean fastest

You don't care about distance. You care about time. So the edge weights become travel times, and the heuristic has to become a time that never overestimates: the straight-line distance divided by the maximum speed allowed anywhere on the graph, ||[h_{\text{time}}(v) = \frac{\text{straight-line distance}(v, t)}{v_{\max}}.||]This guess is honest, but it's a huge underestimate. It assumes you could drive at highway speed along the straight line, even through a residential maze. A weak heuristic means a flat "hill", and A* falls back to behaving like Dijkstra, while it still pays for computing ||(h||) (and in the real world, a square root) at every node. Peter Sanders, in the video: for travel time, A* loses against a well-tuned Dijkstra. In the grid below, sandy cells are highways that are 4× faster when you optimise travel time, so ||(h||) is divided by 4.

Hint: \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(v_{\\max}||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e in the formula only exists because highways exist.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Search from both ends

Run one Dijkstra forward from the source and one backward from the target, always growing the side whose next node is cheaper. If the two points are ||(R||) apart, a single search covers a disc of area about ||(\pi R^2||). Two searches each reach about ||(R/2||): ||[2\cdot \pi\left(\tfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac12\,\pi R^2 .||]That's half the work, and sometimes better. The stopping rule is subtle. Keep ||(\mu||) = the best complete path seen where the two searches touch, and stop once ||(\text{top}_{\text{fwd}} + \text{top}_{\text{bwd}} \ge \mu||). Stopping the moment the two frontiers meet is a classic bug, because the first meeting point is not always on the shortest path. In the video, Carnegie Hall → Wall Street went from about 7,200 explored nodes to about 2,600, close to 3× fewer.

Bidirectional search is a big win, but it's still\n\u003cstrong\u003ehierarchy-blind\u003c/strong\u003e. As Ben Strasser puts it, it will still check whether driving halfway into the In-N-Out drive-through gives a shorter path.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Road hierarchy and the pre-processing trade-off

Humans don't route like Dijkstra. You meander out on local roads, hop on a highway, and hop off near the destination. Early in-car GPS units (1990s) hard-coded this. Surveyors labelled every road (express highway / major local road / narrow road). The device ran a bidirectional Dijkstra on narrow roads inside a small candidate area, then moved up a level, and then up again to highways. The flaw: how big should the candidate area be? If it's too small, you get a highway route when a chain of local roads was really shorter. If it's too large, you're back to Dijkstra. Nothing proves the answer is the shortest. The deeper idea is a trade-off between pre-processing time and query time. At one extreme, precompute every shortest path into a giant lookup table. At the other, precompute nothing and run Dijkstra. Google needs queries under a millisecond with reasonable pre-processing.

data.text/markdown:
6 · Contraction hierarchies: rank the nodes, add shortcuts, search only upward

Instead of humans labelling roads, the computer ranks every node by importance:
  • Nested dissection. Find a small set of nodes that cuts the graph roughly in half: the bridge between two towns, or the 102 Mississippi crossings that split North America. Give them the highest ranks. Then recurse into each half (the Ohio River, the Rockies, …) until every node is ranked.
  • Contract from the bottom. "Pull down" the nodes in rank order. When you contract node ||(v||), look at its neighbours with higher rank. Every pair ||(a, b||) forms a lower triangle ||(a - v - b||). Add a shortcut ||(a - b||) with weight ||(w(a,v)+w(v,b)||). If an edge ||(a - b||) already exists, keep the minimum.
  • Query. Run a bidirectional Dijkstra where each side may only move up the hierarchy. The two searches meet near the top. Answer ||(=\min_x \big(d_\uparrow(s,x)+d_\uparrow(t,x)\big)||).
Without shortcuts, the upward-only search misses paths that dip through lower-ranked nodes (the video's "cost 15, but there is a path that costs 3"). Shortcuts are exactly those dips, precomputed. In the stepper, the number inside each node is its rank (higher = more important), and the vertical position follows the rank too.

data.text/markdown:
7 · A bad ranking is slow, a good one is logarithmic

The video's cleanest example is a road that is just a line of nodes.
  • Contract left to right: no shortcuts are needed at all, but a query between the two ends must climb through every node. That's no better than Dijkstra.
  • Nested dissection: the middle node gets the top rank, then the middles of each half, and so on. Every node's upward search is a short climb of about ||(\log_2 n||) steps. The price is a few extra shortcuts.
"You want this trade-off between the number of shortcuts that you introduce and how much faster the query gets."

8 · Sandbox: build your own city

Everything is switched on: paint walls and highways, drag S and T, and pick the algorithm, objective, and heuristic weight. The table re-runs all algorithms on your map. Some challenges:
  • Build a map where A* explores more than half of what Dijkstra explores, even with distance as the objective.
  • Build a map where bidirectional search is worse than one-way Dijkstra.
  • Use a highway grid and time. Find the w at which A*'s path stops being the fastest.

data.text/markdown:
Recap

Idea Rule What it buys Weak spot
Brute force try every route trivially correct ||(\sim10^{220}||) routes
BFS explore 1 step, 2 steps, … away fewest edges ignores road lengths
Dijkstra (1956) explore the cheapest unexplored node; relax ||(\min(\text{cost}(v), \text{cost}(u)+w)||) shortest path, no pre-processing floods in all directions (≈ 7 s on North America)
A* order by ||(\text{cost} + w\,h||) ≈ 10× fewer nodes for distance weak ||(h||) for travel time
Bidirectional grow from both ends, stop when ||(\text{top}_f+\text{top}_b \ge \mu||) ≈ ½ the area still hierarchy-blind
Manual road classes (1990s GPS) search local → major → highway in candidate areas fast no guarantee of the shortest path
Contraction hierarchy (CCH) nested-dissection ranks + bottom-up shortcuts + upward bidirectional Dijkstra ≈ 200 µs queries, 35,000× faster, exact hours of pre-processing; phase 2 reruns for traffic
At its core, every one of these is still Dijkstra's 20-minute invention. "Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability." (Edsger W. Dijkstra)
